title: Brownian arrival pulse lab notes
content:
Objective:
Quick, messy log of a Brownian-style arrival pattern + pulse perturbation experiment. Goal: understand microburst tail behavior and interactions with prefix/KV cache priming under quantized 4-bit model on mixed GPU pool. Not for share yet — notes to self and Aisha/Evan.

Hypothesis:
- Brownian arrival (small random hops) keeps KV cache 'partially warm' and is less harmful than sudden full pulses.
- Superimposed short pulses (50–200reqs over 200–800ms) will reveal non-linear tail amplification when concurrency limit hit + cold KV shards.
- Priming a tiny set of prefixes (top-10) before pulses should reduce p99 by ~20–35% without a large cost increase.

Environment / config:
- Model: rw-infer/open-4b-quant (4-bit QAT-like build)
- Serving runtime: canary runtime-optimized build (kernel-selection v3)
- HW: mixed pool, 4x A10G + 2x T4 simulated (T4 used for background load)
- Quantization: 4-bit, grouped per-128
- Batch config: dynamic batching enabled, max_batch=64, batch_timeout_ms=12
- Concurrency: per-GPU concurrency limit=16
- KV cache: enabled, per-tenant shards=8, TTL=30m, priming allowed
- Traffic generator: local pulse-generator (python) with Brownian jitter process + Poisson baseline
- Metrics collected: p50/p95/p99, mean latency, qps, GPU util, queue depth, batch size distribution, KV hit rate

Test plan (runs):
1) Baseline Brownian-only: mean qps=220, sigma small hops (brownian_step=±15%), no pulses, no priming. 10m run.
2) Add short pulses: inject 4 pulses/min, each pulse = 120–180 reqs over 300–700ms. 20m run.
3) Primed prefixes: same as (2) but prewarm top-10 prefixes (single prefix warm-up calls 30s prior). 20m run.
4) Stress T4 background: repeat (2) with 2x T4 background noise to emulate noisy tenant. 15m run.
5) Max-batching-off: run (2) with max_batch=1 to isolate batching effects. 10m run.

Quick log of observed results (raw skim):
- Run1 (brownian baseline):
  qps mean: 215
  p50: 15 ms
  p95: 43 ms
  p99: 112 ms
  kv_hit_rate: 56% (warm fraction fluctuating 45–68%)
  avg batch size: 4.6
  note: steady-state, no large queues, occasional 1–2x spike when brownian hops cluster.

- Run2 (pulses enabled):
  qps mean: 260 (pulses bump to 520 for 0.5s)
  p50: 17 ms
  p95: 70 ms
  p99: 310 ms (bad)
  kv_hit_rate: 49% during pulses (drops sharply)
  batch size: avg 5.2, but many tiny batches during delta
  queue depth: spikes to 22 for ~600ms in worst pulse
  observation: p99 increases nonlinearly when concurrency limit reached; tail correlated with KV miss storms and small-batch amplification.

- Run3 (prefix priming):
  qps mean: 258
  p50: 16 ms
  p95: 58 ms
  p99: 190 ms (≈39% reduction vs run2)
  kv_hit_rate: 68% for primed prefixes, overall 61%
  batch size: slightly higher avg 5.6 (fewer tiny batches)
  note: priming reduced tail significantly but not eliminated the hit-rate cliff for non-primed prefixes.

- Run4 (T4 background noisy tenants):
  qps mean: 255 (background load + jitter)
  p50: 19 ms
  p95: 95 ms
  p99: 430 ms (worse than run2)
  gpu util: A10G ~78% steady, T4 fluctuating 55–90%
  note: interference on shared PCI / memory bandwidth suspected; added variance in kernel selection.

- Run5 (max_batch=1):
  qps mean: 240
  p50: 8 ms (single-request path faster for short requests)
  p95: 120 ms
  p99: 520 ms (huge!)
  observation: disabling batching reduced median but exploded tail — likely because batching helps amortize kernel startup costs and KV fetchs for bursts.

Quick transcript observations / micro-insights:
- Tail amplification mechanism hypothesis: when a pulse hits and concurrency caps, inflight requests are buffered -> batcher emits many small batches under timeout -> for miss-heavy requests we do a per-request KV fetch/alloc path that incurs ~80–150ms overhead amplified by serialization.
- The KV miss storm seems to be the main driver. If hit-rate falls below ~55%, tail grows rapidly.
- Priming top-10 prefixes helped because they cover ~42% of pulse traffic in this synthetic workload. In real workloads top-k skew will matter; priming budget should be adaptive.
- Background T4 noise suggests we should add mem-bandwidth / p2p metrics to telemetry. GPU util alone is insufficient.

Immediate actions / experiments to run next (ordered):
- Instrument per-request KV fetch latency distribution; add histogram to tracing. (low effort)
- Try priming top-50 prefixes but with staggered timing to avoid priming storm. Measure p99 vs cost delta.
- Add micro-delay coalescer: when queue depth > threshold, introduce a tiny coalescing window (2–6ms) to form larger batches. Test effect on median & tail.
- Run same pulses on fully-dedicated A100 cluster to compare infra noise.
- For T4 interference: repeat with isolated PCI lanes (if available) or move noisy T4s to different node pool.

Notes to self / debugging hints:
- When reproducing, set seed on Brownian generator; runs here used seed=2741.
- Keep a separate trace id prefix for priming requests (trace:PRM-) so we can filter them later.
- Check kernel selection logs around worst pulses (+/- 5s) for unexpected fallback to slower kernels.
- Related GHPR#4621 touches batcher timeout heuristics — might be relevant.

Rough cost estimate of priming approach (back-of-envelope):
- Priming top-10 prefixes every 5m -> ~1000 extra requests / hour (small cheap calls).
- If p99 improvement reduces SRE incident time by 1–2h/month, worth it for most customers. Need to formalize for pricing.

Final quick verdict (scratchpad):
- Brownian arrival alone is fine. Pulses reveal a tail dominated by KV miss storms + small-batch amplification.
- Prefix priming is an effective mitigation for skewed pulse patterns; best used adaptively.
- Batch coalescing + KV fetch path optimization should be high priority before recommending priming at scale.

TODO (next week):
- Add per-prefix frequency counter in telemetry.
- Implement simple coalescer patch and run A/B against current batcher.
- Run same test on canary A100 nodes and collect p99 delta.

-- Ronan
(tiny, messy log; will clean into a short postmortem if/when this becomes canonical)
